narrative:
Your application was reviewed by a predictive model that assessed your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and the model estimated a 51% probability that you would not pass — a result that sits right on the edge of the decision boundary, meaning your situation is genuinely close to qualifying. Because the model predicted you would fail, your application was unfortunately rejected. It's important to understand that this is not a final judgment of your abilities, but rather a signal about where targeted improvement could make a meaningful difference.

To help explain this decision, the model explored a series of "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile where certain factors were different enough to flip the prediction from "will fail" to "will pass." These counterfactual scenarios are not about who you are, but about what changes in your circumstances or preparation could lead to a more favorable outcome. Think of them as a roadmap showing the shortest path from rejection to approval.

Across all three alternative scenarios the model generated, one factor changed every single time: your LSAT score. No other factor — not your undergraduate GPA, not your law school grades, not your enrollment status, not your family income — changed in any of the scenarios. This makes the LSAT the single most decisive lever in your case. On average, the scenarios required your LSAT score to increase by 2 points, moving from your current score of 34 to 36.

This finding is striking because your profile has genuine strengths that the model already recognizes. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is actually well above the average of 3.24 among students who passed the bar, which is a real asset. The model did not ask you to change your GPA in any scenario — it's already working in your favor. Similarly, your enrollment status, family income, and law school grades were left untouched across all scenarios, suggesting the model is not penalizing those factors enough to require change.

That said, your law school academic performance does stand out as an area of concern in context. Students who passed the bar averaged around a 6th-decile ranking in their first year and similarly in their third year, while your rankings of 3rd and 1st decile respectively are notably below those benchmarks. While the model didn't ask you to change these in the counterfactuals — likely because the LSAT adjustment alone was sufficient — improving your class standing would likely strengthen your position further.

The most actionable takeaway is clear and concrete: raising your LSAT score by just 2 points, from 34 to 36, appears to be the minimum change needed to shift the model's prediction in your favor. Given how close your current probability of failure is to 50%, this is an achievable target. Focused LSAT preparation — particularly through timed practice tests and targeted work on your weaker question types — could realistically close that gap. Your strong undergraduate academic record suggests you have the foundational capability to do so.
